articles.title: How Gaza war sped up India’s shift towards Israel under Modi
articles.summary: As even Israel's traditional allies are distancing themselves from Netanyahu, Modi's India has embraced the country.
articles.preview: As even Israel’s traditional allies are distancing themselves from Netanyahu, Modi’s India has embraced the country. New Delhi, India – The United Kingdom, France, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Norway had already banned the entry of Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s far-right finance minister, who had advocated the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in Gaza and the annexation of the occupied West Bank.
articles.body:
As even Israel’s traditional allies are distancing themselves from Netanyahu, Modi’s India has embraced the country.

New Delhi, India – The United Kingdom, France, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Norway had already banned the entry of Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s far-right finance minister, who had advocated the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in Gaza and the annexation of the occupied West Bank.

But in September 2025, as the European Union was planning bloc-wide sanctions against him and his fellow far-right colleague Itamar Ben-Gvir that it would eventually announce late that month, Smotrich was welcomed with garlands and a multi-city trip to India. In New Delhi, he signed a trade deal; in Mumbai, he visited the stock exchange; and in Gujarat – the home state of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi – he travelled to a new investment hub.

As Israel was conducting its genocidal war on Gaza, bombing and killing dozens on the very days he was visiting India, New Delhi was ready to expand business with Israel like never before. For decades, India had been one of the world’s staunchest supporters of Palestine, and Europe one of Israel’s closest backers. India’s position has shifted firmly since 2014, when Modi and his Hindu majoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party came to power. But analysts say the optics of Smotrich’s visit underlined something even more dramatic: At a time when even Europe, traditionally seen as backing Israel, has veered away from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, the genocidal war on Gaza appears to have escalated India’s embrace of Israel.

In February this year, Modi visited Israel as Netanyahu – who faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court over war crimes carried out in Gaza – faced growing isolation in the international arena.

“You are a great friend of Israel. You are more than a friend. You are a brother,” Netanyahu told Modi when both leaders addressed the Israeli parliament in Jerusalem.

How October 7 attack changed tones

Three years of Israeli attacks have killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children. That is about one in every 30 people, or 3 percent of the pre-war population.

Historically, India has argued that diplomacy and dialogue are the way forward to resolve conflicts – whether between Russia and Ukraine, the US and Iran, or Israel and Palestine. New Delhi has maintained that war doesn’t solve anything.

But investigations by Al Jazeera and other reporting have revealed that New Delhi exported weapons to Israel during the ongoing genocidal war on Gaza. Meanwhile, under Modi, India has become Israel’s largest weapons buyer.

Just hours after the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, India’s Modi unequivocally condemned the “terrorist attack”, adding that he was “deeply shocked”. When he visited Israel in February this year, Modi referred to the Mumbai attacks in 2008, carried out by Pakistani fighters, which New Delhi has blamed on the Pakistani government. “Like you, we have a consistent and uncompromising policy of zero tolerance for terrorism with no double standards,” Modi said.

Analysts believe that the framing of Israel as a country under attack has helped Modi justify pushing India closer to it. For decades, much of the politics of Modi’s BJP “has hovered around Islamist expansionism or Islamic terrorism”, said Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst in New Delhi.

“So it helps [in relationship with Israel],” Kidwai said, pointing to the link between Modi’s Israel policy and his domestic politics. “Take this relationship as an extension of the domestic narrative that one sees in India.”

The Indian Hindu right has long supported the ideology of Zionism, analysts note. Modi’s BJP has roots in a philosophy, Hindutva, which ultimately seeks to transform India into a Hindu nation and a natural homeland for Hindus anywhere in the world – similar to Israel’s view of itself as a Jewish homeland.

Since the October 7 attacks on Israel, Kidwai noted, “the anti-Muslim sentiments fill in that block in India.” This feeling is, of course, coupled with “pragmatism in New Delhi because Israel is a potent international player”.

Navdeep Suri, a former Indian diplomat who served as ambassador to Egypt and the United Arab Emirates, told Al Jazeera that people-to-people ties are also a central pillar of the India-Israel relationship, “particularly within a section of Indian society that has strong admiration for the muscular policy that Israel adopts”.

Time and again, there have been calls from within Indian right-wing echelons for Modi to adopt more Israel-like policies, from clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir to attacking neighbouring Pakistan.

Suri noted that a shift towards Israel predates the ongoing genocidal war in Gaza. “Under PM Modi, a relationship that was largely covert or under the carpet has become a much more open relationship,” the former Indian diplomat said.

“There has been a recognition in Delhi that Israel has been a very strong defence and intelligence partner,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to another pillar of the bilateral relationship. “There’s a genuine convergence when it comes to the perceptions on security.”

India ‘should take principled positions’

Even several of Israel’s closest European allies have moved from criticism of the genocidal war on Gaza and expansive illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank to concrete measures. At least 11 European countries and Canada have imposed trade measures against products from illegal Israeli settlements. Many have imposed sanctions on settlers and networks accused of conducting pogroms against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, as well as on ministers like Smotrich and Ben-Gvir.

India, for its part, has avoided anything more than homilies and mild opposition to war and West Bank attacks.

Diplomatically, New Delhi still backs a two-state solution and has called for aid access and peace in the region. Suri, the former Indian diplomat who served in the Middle East, said New Delhi “should be able to take more principled positions on these things”.

However, from his experience in office, Suri added, “there is such a close alignment at the political levels between the governments in Israel and India that there is a reluctance [in India] to criticise Israel.

“That reluctance manifests in various aspects,” Suri explained to Al Jazeera. “The refusal to criticise the settlers’ attacks; refusal to criticise the brutal use of force in Gaza; refusal to criticise the attack on Iran and point out violation of international norms.”

Unlike Western countries, India’s current leaders “lack that kind of dynamic thinking and are rather far more dogmatic”, said Kidwai, the political analyst.

India’s shift and Modi’s calculus

Netanyahu’s disruptive and fatal assault on Gaza has drawn ire from even the White House in Washington, where Israel enjoys bipartisan support. United States President Donald Trump has previously threatened to cut off support for Israel’s bombing of Lebanon – even while signing off on huge weapons sales to Israel.

However, nothing has moved Modi’s bonhomie with Israel’s Netanyahu.

In fact, Modi’s February visit on the eve of the joint US-Israel attacks on Iran appeared “as almost a personal favour to Netanyahu by boosting his image as an international statesman just as Israeli election campaigning is getting under way”, Max Rodenbeck, Israel/Palestine programme director at the Washington-based International Crisis Group, had told Al Jazeera.

Such an act would have been unthinkable from an Indian leader in previous decades.

In 1948, India opposed the creation of Israel. A relationship with Israel was once frowned upon in New Delhi – a legacy of India’s anti-colonial past – though the two had clandestine ties since at least the 1970s.

India backed the 1975 United Nations General Assembly resolution calling Zionism a form of racism, was the first non-Arab nation to recognise the Palestine Liberation Organization, and was among the first in the world to recognise Palestinian statehood. It only established diplomatic ties with Israel in 1992, and though governments since then slowly built up relations, Modi, in 2016, was the first Indian PM to visit that country.

The Congress party that’s now in opposition, but ruled India for most of its post-independence period before Modi, also viewed its support for Palestine as helpful with Muslim voters – only Indonesia and Pakistan have more Muslims than India – said Kidwai. Modi’s Hindu-first politics, by contrast, thrives on othering Indian Muslims.

“Modi’s party believes it stands to gain nothing from a pro-Palestine posture,” Kidwai told Al Jazeera. “Instead, Modi has sought to link the attack on Israel with the so-called reign of terror and Islamic extremism and make a case against Muslims – and within those realms lies the justification of everything.”

articles.title: Most UK diplomats to leave East Jerusalem consulate, Israel says, as Miliband says 'vital services' to remain
articles.summary: Israel said in September it would act in response to UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
articles.preview: Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission". "We did not want it to come to this," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social media, as he said 20 diplomats and the consul general would leave Israel while a task force of seven could remain in the building "with a very limited scope of activity".
articles.body:
Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission".

"We did not want it to come to this," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social media, as he said 20 diplomats and the consul general would leave Israel while a task force of seven could remain in the building "with a very limited scope of activity".

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband responded that some staff had been "temporarily withdrawn" for security reasons, but stressed the mission will "work with the Palestinian people".

Israel said in September it would shut the consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law.

The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate ahead of Thursday's deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement.

The consulate, which was first established in 1838, handles UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.

It is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK's main diplomatic hub with Israel.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the country had implemented measures announced on 8 September in response to UK sanctions.

"The British Consulate in Jerusalem is closing its operations today. Accordingly, the sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed," he wrote on social media.

However, the British flag could still be seen outside on Thursday morning, and several staff were seen entering.

Saar said talks with the UK government had resulted in agreement on certain principles, including that "the consul general and 20 diplomats (including the consul general) are ending their duties and will leave Israel."

But Saar acknowledged that the building is "the property of the British government" and said Israel had authorised "a task force of only seven diplomats with a very limited scope of activity" to operate in the building.

As a result of this agreement with the UK, he said, "no steps will be taken against Israel".

Israeli media had been reporting that the UK had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats from London - raising the prospect of further damaging bilateral relations.

This agreement is a compromise of sorts and means - for the moment - the heat has been taken out of a dispute that could have further worsened UK-Israel relations.

Israel can claim that the British Consulate is "closing its operations". A score of British diplomats, including the consul general, are leaving.

But Miliband says they are going only temporarily and only for their safety and security. He continues to insist Israel has no legal right to close the consulate.

"The UK government reiterates its long-standing view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory," Miliband wrote in a statement.

Following discussions with the Israeli government, he said, the building "will not be closing" and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from Thursday.

However Miliband said an understanding had not been reached on "necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises".

"Accordingly the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security," he added.

The Foreign Office said the seven UK diplomats who remain will be "independent and operational" and continue to deliver vital services. Israel said they will provide "only a limited scope of activity".

FCDO sources described the deal as a "good outcome" because the entire operation was not closing, as had been threatened. They said that maintaining a UK presence would help build back the mission in the future.

Speaking to the Today programme, Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty explained: "The building remains open. We retain our presence, we continue having staff able to do important work engaging with the Palestinian Authority... and we are engaging in ongoing conversations with Israel on this matter."

Asked if this was a political fudge, Doughty said "you can see what's changed in terms of a name but crucially our presence remains", adding that the "policies towards this Israeli government, which we fundamentally disagree with" would continue.

The foreign secretary made clear the UK reserved the right to take what he called "reciprocal action" but said he would not do so while "discussions are under way and credible". That means any UK retaliation is unlikely before Israel's elections later this month.

articles.title: Why Israel loves skunk water
articles.summary: Israel’s foul-smelling weapon turns Palestinian repression into a sales pitch.
articles.preview: Israel’s foul-smelling weapon turns Palestinian repression into a sales pitch. In the eyes of Israeli authorities, Palestinians in Gaza have it “too good”. Three years into Israel’s genocide, the survivors have been pushed into ever smaller areas of land amid rubble, rubbish and disease, without adequate shelter or sanitation. Apparently, even that is too much. In late September, a foul smell spread across Gaza City overnight.
articles.body:
Israel’s foul-smelling weapon turns Palestinian repression into a sales pitch.

In the eyes of Israeli authorities, Palestinians in Gaza have it “too good”. Three years into Israel’s genocide, the survivors have been pushed into ever smaller areas of land amid rubble, rubbish and disease, without adequate shelter or sanitation. Apparently, even that is too much.

In late September, a foul smell spread across Gaza City overnight. At first, residents searched for its source around them, wondering whether it was coming from a toilet or even one of their sleeping children. Then reports of the same stench began coming in from across the city. Israeli aircraft had reportedly dropped hundreds of packets containing a foul-smelling substance over populated areas.

“Today, all of us in Gaza City woke up to a foul, rotten smell in the truest sense of the word … Israeli occupation drones were spraying this foul stench to pollute the air. Even the air?” said one witness to AJ+.

Israel has, in fact, spent nearly two decades weaponising foul smells against Palestinians.

Skunk water, the leading Israeli olfactory ordnance now believed to be in use in Gaza, was developed in 2004 by the Israeli company Odortec in partnership with Israel Police’s Technological Development Department, and first deployed against Palestinian protesters in Nilin in 2008. It is classified as a “scent-based non-lethal weapon” for crowd control and can be fired from water cannon or dropped from drones.

From Nilin, its use spread across the occupied West Bank. It became a regular feature of demonstrations in Bilin, Kafr Qaddum and Nabi Saleh, where Israeli forces repeatedly used it against Palestinians protesting settlements, land seizures and restrictions on movement. In 2011, Israeli forces fired tear gas and skunk water on unarmed demonstrators who had attended the burial of a 28-year-old killed by the Israeli army in Nabi Saleh and were then making their way to the village spring that had been “appropriated by the neighbouring settlement, Halamish”. Similar incidents were reported there in 2012 and 2013.

The practice soon spread beyond those West Bank villages. In 2013, activists demonstrating against the closure of Shuhada Street in Hebron and journalists covering the protest were sprayed with the putrid liquid. The following year, Israeli police drove skunk trucks through Palestinian neighbourhoods in East Jerusalem, spraying homes, streets and schools. In at-Tur, four schools were hit, forcing some 4,500 pupils to stay home because of the smell.

By 2018, Israel was also deploying it from the air. During the Great March of Return, the Israeli military used the Shoko drone to douse Palestinian protesters in Gaza with the foul-smelling liquid from a payload of plastic bags.

For Israeli authorities, its usefulness goes well beyond crowd control. Sure, spray it on a protest and people scatter. But spray it over streets, homes and neighbourhoods, and it becomes a tool for making Palestinian space itself unliveable.

That goes some way towards explaining Israel’s enduring enthusiasm for skunk water. There is another reason, too: Israel sells to the world the methods it has developed to control Palestinians.

When skunk water was first deployed in 2008, it was reported that Israeli police had “high hopes of turning it into a commercial venture and selling it to law-enforcement agencies overseas”. Superintendent David Ben Harosh even went on air hugging a “litre bottle of dirty, green liquid” and boasting: “It’s totally harmless, you can even drink it.”

Its use against Palestinians – whom Israel has long characterised as a symbol of pathological evil – also feeds the country’s global reputation as a pioneer of counterinsurgency and policing technologies. Every deployment offers another demonstration of Israeli expertise in controlling the population it presents as uniquely dangerous.

By then, Israel had already begun exporting it. In 2007, Beit Alfa Technologies supplied skunk water to the South African Police Service along with “water cannons and riot-control gear”. These were later used against demonstrators during the Fees Must Fall protests in 2015.

In 2017, India’s Central Reserve Police Force tested skunk water for crowd control in places including Jammu and Kashmir. The Who Profits Research Center has also said it was approached by a company seeking help contacting Odortec to buy the liquid for sale to Colombian police.

In the United States, Mistral Security supplies skunk water, claiming that “the stench of Skunk immediately causes individuals and crowds to cease their activities while allowing Law Enforcement to gain control with minimum injuries and casualties”.

The company’s marketing makes the connection to Palestine unusually explicit: its website uses a photograph of Israeli forces deploying skunk water against Palestinians in the West Bank. The Palestinians subjected to the weapon become part of the proof that it works.

Following the 2014 Ferguson protests, Mistral supplied skunk water to several US police departments. This included the St Louis Metropolitan Police Department in Missouri, which acquired the liquid in 2015 following the protests in Ferguson.

A Quartz report on the shipment to Missouri captured what makes the weapon attractive. “The poisoning of a place”, it observed, can destroy people’s willingness to “reside, congregate, protest, or even document a location” until it is cleaned away. It described skunk water as potentially “a system for maintaining new apartheids”.

What Israel sells, then, is more than a foul-smelling liquid. Skunk water comes wrapped in the reputation Israel has built through decades of controlling Palestinians: a state presented as uniquely experienced in suppressing unrest, countering insurgency and dealing with populations cast as dangerous. Palestinians are central to that brand. Their repression demonstrates the technology; their demonisation helps justify the expertise built around controlling them.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Axios: 'Ordine alle forze armate Usa per un'eventuale ripresa degli attacchi all'Iran'
articles.summary: Trump non ha ancora preso decisioni. Ipotesi prima delle midterm e delle elezioni in Israele
articles.preview: Il Pentagono ha dato alcuni giorni fa istruzioni al Comando centrale degli Stati Uniti (Centcom) di completare i preparativi per la ripresa delle operazioni di combattimento su larga scala contro l'Iran. Lo riporta Axios, citando funzionari Usa. La direttiva non indicava una data specifica per l'avvio degli attacchi e il presidente Donald Trump non ha ancora preso decisioni definitive.
articles.body:
Il Pentagono ha dato alcuni giorni fa istruzioni al Comando centrale degli Stati Uniti (Centcom) di completare i preparativi per la ripresa delle operazioni di combattimento su larga scala contro l'Iran. Lo riporta Axios, citando funzionari Usa.

La direttiva non indicava una data specifica per l'avvio degli attacchi e il presidente Donald Trump non ha ancora preso decisioni definitive. Tuttavia, fonti di Usa e Israele hanno affermato che l'azione potrebbe avvenire prima delle midterm di novembre e, forse, prima delle elezioni israeliane di una settimana prima. Nel mirino, obiettivi energetici, infrastrutturali e nucleari iraniani.

La ripresa del conflitto nelle prossime 3 o 4 settimane potrebbe influenzare le elezioni di metà mandato Usa, in parte a causa del possibile aumento dei prezzi del petrolio. "Il compito del Dipartimento è elaborare e presentare opzioni militari al Presidente", ha dichiarato un funzionario del Pentagono ad Axios. Mentre un altro della Casa Bianca ha affermato che Trump ha tutte le opzioni a disposizione in qualsiasi momento: "gli Stati Uniti si trovano in una posizione di grande forza, controllando lo Stretto di Hormuz mentre l'economia iraniana sta collassando" e "il presidente ha in mano tutte le carte e farà ciò che è meglio per gli Stati Uniti".

Venerdì, il team per la sicurezza nazionale di Trump si è riunito a Camp David per diverse ore allo scopo di discutere di guerra e altre questioni. Un funzionario israeliano ha detto che parte della riunione è stata dedicata alla possibile ripresa di operazioni di combattimento su larga scala in Iran. Dopo l'incontro, il segretario di Stato Marco Rubio ha detto che la discussione è stata riservata a pianificare la politica estera a "lungo termine", con lo stallo negoziale Usa-Iran.

Ieri Trump ha parlato con il premier israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu. Si è trattato della loro seconda conversazione in pochi giorni, dopo un lungo periodo di scarso contatto. Un funzionario Usa ha riferito che i due hanno discusso di "memoria e rispetto per le vittime del massacro del 7 ottobre".

Qualora dovessero riprendere le operazioni di combattimento su larga scala, è molto probabile che possa vedere Stati Uniti e Israele agire in tandem, con la partecipazione diretta delle forze armate israeliane. Una nuova escalation - o anche solo un inasprimento della tensione o dello stato di emergenza - potrebbe avvantaggiare Netanyahu sul piano politico, impedendo agli avversari di attaccarlo nella fase conclusiva della campagna elettorale.

Continua ad aggravarsi il bilancio dell'attacco russo che ieri ha colpito un palazzo residenziale a Pryluky, nella regione ucraina di Chernihiv. "Questa mattina, il bilancio è di 22 morti, tra cui cinque bambini. Altre 54 persone sono rimaste ferite, tra cui 7 bambini", ha riferito su Telegram il Servizio statale di emergenza dell'Ucraina.

"Durante le operazioni di soccorso, i soccorritori sono riusciti a salvare 15 persone, tra cui un bambino. Attualmente, le squadre di soccorso continuano a rimuovere le macerie e a smantellare le strutture distrutte", ha aggiunto.

E i raid e le vittime non si fermano: due persone sono morte a seguito di un altro attacco russo che ieri sera ha colpito un palazzo nel quartiere di Desnyanskyi di Kiev. Lo afferma il Servizio statale di emergenza ucraino, ricordando che il raid ha provocato un incendio e la parziale distruzione delle strutture fino al decimo piano.

"In uno degli appartamenti danneggiati, i vigili del fuoco hanno trovato i corpi di due persone decedute. Sono state tratte in salvo 22 persone, tra cui 8 bambini. Inoltre, 4 persone sono rimaste ferite, tra cui 2 bambini", ha riferito il servizio su Telegram.

Un incendio è scoppiato nei pressi della raffineria di petrolio Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat, nella repubblica russa del Baschiria, a seguito di un attacco. Lo scrivono i media ucraini, tra cui Rbc e Ukrainska Pravda, citando canali Telegram che rilanciano immagini del rogo. Stando a quanto riferito, l'incendio sarebbe divampato a diversi chilometri dalla città, probabilmente vicino alla raffineria, come suggerito dall'analisi delle immagini.

Si tratta di uno dei più grandi complessi russi di raffinazione del petrolio e petrolchimici, situato nella città di Salavat che dista 1.400 km dal confine con l'Ucraina. La struttura era già stata in precedenza bersaglio di attacchi con droni: i media ucraini riportano che Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat lavora fino a 10 milioni di tonnellate di idrocarburi all'anno e produce oltre 150 tipi di prodotti, tra cui benzina, gasolio, olio combustibile, bitume, polietilene, stirene e ammoniaca.

articles.title: How October 7 redrew the map of the Middle East
articles.summary: Three years of war have upended alliances, weakened US influence and reshaped the region’s power balance.
articles.preview: Three years of war have upended alliances, weakened US influence and reshaped the region’s power balance. In the past three years, following the October 7 attacks and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the wider region has been marked by conflict, economic turmoil, and a shattering of the balance of power. The network of alliances maintained by Iran, long central to its regional power, has been hit hard and severely weakened. Yemen’s Houthi rebels remain one notable exception.
articles.body:
Three years of war have upended alliances, weakened US influence and reshaped the region’s power balance.

In the past three years, following the October 7 attacks and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the wider region has been marked by conflict, economic turmoil, and a shattering of the balance of power.

The network of alliances maintained by Iran, long central to its regional power, has been hit hard and severely weakened. Yemen’s Houthi rebels remain one notable exception.

Israel has made gains. Many of the leaders of the Lebanese group Hezbollah and the Palestinian group Hamas have been killed, while Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was also assassinated in February. Israel occupies most of Gaza, where it has also killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and reduced much of the enclave to rubble.

Its military aggression has come at a cost, isolating it from its traditional allies and making it globally unpopular, including in the United States. The potential for more normalisation deals with Arab countries seems unlikely, at least in the short term.

Instead, Israel continues to launch attacks across the region, crossing previously held red lines – such as the 2025 attack on Doha, Qatar – and making many governments around the world view it as the primary source of unrest in the Middle East.

US not a protector

“Before October 7, the US’s entire policy in the Middle East rested on normalising Israel’s presence in the region through its so-called Abraham Accords,” HA Hellyer of the Royal United Services Institute said, referring to the normalisation deals with several Arab states, including the United Arab Emirates. “Israel’s response to the October 7 attack ended that.”

Instead, rather than a stable Middle East with Israel at its centre, the US entered into a war with Iran this year, and has since looked on as Tehran targeted US allies across the Gulf, shattering the perceived security of the US security umbrella.

Drones and missiles hit Qatar’s Ras Laffan gas hub and started fires near Dubai airport and at Fujairah’s oil zone. In September, the Houthis surged down Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking the port of Mocha and nearby islands. Their gains tightened their grip on the Bab al-Mandeb strait, threatening a key route for global trade and energy supplies that had become even more important amid disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.

“There’s been a loss of faith in the US as a singularly sufficient security guarantor,” Hellyer continued.

“This is why you’re seeing many in the region talk to other external actors, in addition to continuing, and in some cases deepening their US ties, as well as initiatives such as the Mecca security pact as states in the region look elsewhere for ways to safeguard their security,” he said, referring to the defence agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan, signed in August, agreeing that an attack on one was to be regarded as an attack on all.

Alliances

Alongside the loss of confidence in the US as a security guarantor has come a dramatic reordering of alliances and rivalries. Much of Iran’s network – most notably Hezbollah, whose reputation had long served as a deterrent against Israeli attack – appeared to buckle under Israeli pressure.

That, in turn, emboldened an Israeli military push that saw troops invade Lebanon in October 2024 and again in March 2026, and seize Syrian territory during the brief power vacuum that followed Bashar al-Assad’s ouster in 2024.

“The Middle East has always been multi-aligned. However, now it’s even more so,” Sanam Vakil, the director of the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House, said of the increased leverage given to external actors, such as Turkiye in Syria and China’s involvement in negotiations over the end to war on Iran, as Beijing finds its own energy supplies under threat.

“It’s ironic, since October 7, it’s Israel that has emerged as the revisionist power and Iran almost as the status quo power,” she said of the apparent reversal in status of the two belligerents, with Tehran seemingly more focused on regaining the ground it has lost in the last three years rather than advancing beyond them.

However, none of this was to overstate Israeli influence, or liken it to a regional superpower, Vakil cautioned. “Israel may currently be the preponderant military power in the Middle East, but real power is typically classed as being able to project stability, which Israel hasn’t shown itself able or willing to do,” she said.

Clogged arteries

While Israel and the US hoped February’s attacks would swiftly topple Iran’s government, they have instead opened a new front. Tehran now wields economic leverage over Israel, the US and their partners through the Strait of Hormuz, which borders Iran and typically carries about a fifth of the world’s oil and gas, and through Bab al-Mandeb, which is now threatened by its Houthi allies.

Whatever Tehran’s intentions, the economic pain has been uneven. The West, cushioned by emergency reserves, record US oil production and supplies from countries such as Norway, has so far avoided the turmoil of the 1970s oil shocks, when US drivers queued for petrol, even though the current disruption is on a greater scale. In April, the International Monetary Fund trimmed its 2026 global growth forecast only slightly, to 3.1 percent from 3.3 percent.

Gulf exporters, in contrast, have fared far worse. The same assessment cut its forecast for Saudi Arabia from 4.5 to 3.1 percent, and turned Qatar’s from growth of 6.1 percent into a contraction of 8.6 percent.

“It’s curious, in many ways the West’s reduced need for Gulf oil has increased the degree to which Israel has become a liability for the US,” Israeli political economist Shir Hever told Al Jazeera, referring to a diplomatic alliance between the two states long underpinned by Israel’s strategic position in an oil-rich region central to US interests.

“There’s a train of thought in Israel that the current crises may push the Gulf states into allying with it,” he said, while noting the irony that Israel had been the main aggressor in the conflicts that followed October 7. “Though that seems fairly unlikely.”

articles.body:
Un miliardo di euro al giorno, 360 miliardi all’anno. È questa la portata del deficit commerciale europeo nei confronti della Cina, una cifra colossale e insostenibile, soprattutto considerando che interi settori dell’industria europea sono minacciati dalla poderosa macchina di produzione industriale cinese.

L’8 e il 9 ottobre il commissario europeo per il commercio Maroš Šefčovič sarà a Pechino per una serie di incontri che si annunciano molto difficili. Šefčovič parla a nome dei 27, perché il commercio è una prerogativa comunitaria. Il suo obiettivo è duplice: ridurre a ogni costo il deficit ed evitare una guerra commerciale a cui l’Europa non è assolutamente preparata.

Alla vigilia di questo appuntamento cruciale, Francia e Germania hanno allineato le rispettive posizioni. Il 6 ottobre una lettera comune firmata da Emmanuel Macron e Friedrich Merz ha messo fine a mesi di divergenze. La Germania, molto più presente della Francia nel mercato cinese, era più restia all’idea di inasprire i toni, ma ha cambiato idea alla luce del fatto che l’industria cinese sta distruggendo interi settori dell’economia tedesca.

Il linguaggio impiegato nella lettera è piuttosto duro: il testo parla di un “uso del commercio come arma” e di “distorsione sistematica del mercato”. La Cina non è nominata, ma è chiaramente il bersaglio delle accuse. Macron e Merz chiedono alla Commissione europea di creare nuovi strumenti per permettere all’Europa di arginare l’ingresso dei prodotti cinesi.

La lettera è stata diffusa (e non è un caso) alla vigilia della visita a Pechino di Šefčovič, in modo da inviare un messaggio chiaro ai leader cinesi: non potete ignorare il cambio di umore in Europa. Il commissario chiederà a Pechino di adottare misure per limitare alcune esportazioni, per esempio quelle sui veicoli ibridi, ma sappiamo già che il governo cinese si rifiuterà di farlo.

Segno del cambiamento dei toni, l’ex commissario europeo per il commercio Pascal Lamy, lo stesso che nel 2001 aveva negoziato con la Cina il suo ingresso nell’Organizzazione mondiale del commercio, ha rilasciato una serie di interviste in cui ha ammesso di essersi sbagliato sulle intenzioni di Pechino. Su Le Monde ha addirittura parlato di “errore storico”. Anche Lamy propone nuovi strumenti commerciali con cui affrontare la questione.

La Cina resta in posizione di forza, perché la sua superiorità industriale è innegabile. In un libro pubblicato di recente, il ricercatore canadese Dan Wang afferma che il dominio industriale cinese è destinato a durare per una generazione.

Il gigante cinese ha bisogno di sbocchi per la sua produzione, e in questo senso i 450 milioni di consumatori europei non possono essere ignorati. Tuttavia, una guerra commerciale sarebbe un’evoluzione molto pericolosa per l’Europa, che dipende dalla Cina molto più di quanto la Cina dipenda dal mercato europeo. L’anno scorso Pechino ha dimostrato con le restrizioni sulle terre rare di poter piegare perfino Donald Trump e i suoi dazi.

Già alle prese con l’ostilità dell’amministrazione statunitense e con l’aggressività di Vladimir Putin, l’Europa trova nella Cina un avversario temibile su un altro terreno, quello della sopravvivenza economica. Per questo motivo i 27 hanno tutto l’interesse a rafforzare la loro unità, anche oltre il campo della difesa. La lettera franco-tedesca dimostra che i leader europei ne sono ormai consapevoli. ◆

(Traduzione di Andrea Sparacino)

articles.summary: Nel 2026 gli attacchi dei coloni hanno causato più di venti morti e di mille feriti tra i palestinesi. Ufficialmente il premier israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu condanna le violenze, ma il suo governo le incoraggia. Il video di Le Monde
articles.preview: In un post pubblicato sui social media, il ministro delle finanze israeliano e suprematista di estrema destra Bezalel Smotrich distribuisce decine di fuoristrada ai coloni israeliani insediati in Cisgiordania, con l’obiettivo di “garantirne la sicurezza”. L’inchiesta video di Le Monde dimostra che non solo quei veicoli, ma anche le armi automatiche e i droni dati dal governo o dai singoli ministri, sono l’arsenale con cui gli estremisti ebrei attaccano sistematicamente i palestinesi per terrorizzarli e spingerli ad abbandonare terreni e case.
articles.body:
In un post pubblicato sui social media, il ministro delle finanze israeliano e suprematista di estrema destra Bezalel Smotrich distribuisce decine di fuoristrada ai coloni israeliani insediati in Cisgiordania, con l’obiettivo di “garantirne la sicurezza”.

L’inchiesta video di Le Monde dimostra che non solo quei veicoli, ma anche le armi automatiche e i droni dati dal governo o dai singoli ministri, sono l’arsenale con cui gli estremisti ebrei attaccano sistematicamente i palestinesi per terrorizzarli e spingerli ad abbandonare terreni e case. Anche se ufficialmente il primo ministro israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu condanna queste violenze, in realtà il suo governo le incoraggia attivamente, continuando a sostenere materialmente la violenta colonizzazione dei territori palestinesi.

Secondo le Nazioni Unite, nei primi otto mesi del 2026, gli attacchi dei coloni israeliani in Cisgiordania hanno causato 23 morti e 1.100 feriti tra i palestinesi.

articles.title: Three people killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia airports, officials say
articles.summary: The Houthis have claimed responsibility for the attacks, which mark an escalation in the conflict.
articles.preview: Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi Arabia airports over two days, authorities said, as flare-up of fighting spilled across the Yemen border into the kingdom. Two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (Gaca) said in a statement on Wednesday. In a separate incident, one person was killed and eight were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, it added.
articles.body:
Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi Arabia airports over two days, authorities said, as flare-up of fighting spilled across the Yemen border into the kingdom.

Two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (Gaca) said in a statement on Wednesday.

In a separate incident, one person was killed and eight were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, it added.

The attacks, which the Houthis have claimed responsibility for, mark an escalation in the renewed war between the Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

The two airports were attacked on 6 and 7 October, according to Gaca, which did not specify when each airport was hit.

Two women, of Moroccan and Algerian nationalities, were killed during the Abha airport attack, near the Yemen border, according to Gaca.

Meanwhile, a male resident of Sudanese nationality was killed at King Khalid airport, it added.

The country's civil aviation authority did not name who was responsible for the attacks, but Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said its armed forces had attacked both Saudi Arabia airports with ballistic missiles and drones.

The Houthi military spokesperson also said the Houthis attacked Aden's International Airport in Yemen on Wednesday. The airport is a main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside of Houthi control and has been repeatedly targeted when fighting erupts in the country.

Saree said the two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" which saw "60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours".

The civil war in Yemen has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west, seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.

That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping.

But Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.

They also declared an all out war in an effort to take all territory held by the Houthis.

In a statement issued late on Wednesday, the official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports "will not go unpunished".

The spokesperson said the Saudi coalition had targeted more than 80 Houthi military sites across "governorates of Saada, Al Hudaydah, Al Jawf and Ma'rib".

The Saudi-led coalition formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.

A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres has condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting".

Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed on both sides since the latest Houthis' advance.

The UN said on Wednesday more than 200,000 people have been displaced by the escalation.

articles.title: 7 ottobre, Mattarella: "Fermezza contro l'antisemitismo. A Gaza intollerabile devastazione umana"
articles.summary: AGI - "Ignobile" l'attacco di Hamas del 7 ottobre ai civili israeliani. "Di intollerabile gravita'" la "devastazione umana e militare" prodotta dalle operazioni militari israeliane a Gaza" e il "processo di erosione di territori attribuiti all'Autorità Nazionale Palestinese". È una catena di violenza ininterrotta e ugualmente condannabile quella descritta dal Presidente della Repubblica, Sergio Mattarella, nel messaggio in occasione del terzo anniversario della strage del 7 ottobre. Una "spirale di inaudita violenza", è il monito del Capo dello Stato, che "va fermata, ricreando invece i presupposti, oggi profondamente compromessi, della convivenza tra israeliani e palestinesi nella prospettiva 'Due Popoli, Due Stati', per poter vivere pacificamente, fianco a fianco. L'Italia continuerà a sostenere ogni sforzo volto a questo obiettivo", assicura il Presidente. Mattarella: "Vicinanza al popolo di Israele" Una data che "segna la tragica ricorrenza dell'ignobile attacco perpetrato da Hamas contro numerosi civili israeliani", ricorda Mattarella: "Molti giovani, anche di altre nazionalità, vilmente colpiti, tratti in ostaggio o privati della vita mentre si trovavano riuniti per un'occasione di festa. Altri brutalmente uccisi o rapiti nelle loro case, senza nessuna pietà per bambini e anziani". Atti di terrorismo che, sottolinea, "non potranno mai essere giustificati ne' archiviati", ma resteranno, "per tutti i popoli, un doloroso monito affinché siano per sempre condannate e respinte con fermezza, in Medio Oriente e nel mondo intero, le piaghe barbare e incivili del terrorismo, dell'antisemitismo e di ogni forma di odio su base etnica e religiosa". Parole che arrivano a pochi giorni dal ritorno in Aula del disegno di legge per il contrasto all'antisemitismo, il 13 ottobre. "A Gaza devastazione umana intollerabile" Atti "ripugnanti" che, per il Capo dello Stato, hanno aperto la strada una "fase di instabilità e violenze" in tutto la regione, dato che alle "atroci sofferenze causate si aggiungono quelle che, ancor più da allora, gravano su moltitudini di palestinesi. Le operazioni militari condotte dalle forze israeliane a Gaza hanno provocato una devastazione umana e materiale di intollerabile gravita'". A questo, il Presidente Mattarella aggiunge la condanna alle violenze dei coloni Israeliani in Cisgiordania: un "inaccettabile processo di erosione di territori attribuiti all'Autorità Nazionale Palestinese". Da qui il monito affinché sia spezzata questa "spirale di inaudita violenza" e ricreati "i presupposti, oggi profondamente compromessi, della convivenza tra israeliani e palestinesi nella prospettiva 'Due Popoli, Due Stati', per poter vivere pacificamente, fianco a fianco". E l'impegno: "L'Italia continuerà a sostenere ogni sforzo volto a questo obiettivo". Meloni: "Impegno contro l’antisemitismo" Di "spirale di violenza da interrompere" parla anche la presidente del Consiglio, Giorgia Meloni per la quale la data del 7 ottobre deve rappresentare una pietra d'inciampo contro l'antisemitismo: "Il tempo trascorso", prosegue la premier, "non attenua la gravita' di quei crimini. Nessuna causa può giustificare il massacro deliberato di innocenti. Ricordarlo significa anche rinnovare l'impegno contro ogni forma di antisemitismo". "Non siamo indifferenti alle sofferenze del popolo di Gaza" Anche la premier, come già il Capo dello Stato, si sofferma sulle "drammatiche e inaccettabili sofferenze degli abitanti di Gaza" e alla "violenza crescente di cui sono vittime i civili palestinesi in Cisgiordania". Violenze e sofferenze davanti alle quali "non possiamo restare indifferenti". L'orizzonte, ribadisce Meloni, "una pace che garantisca agli israeliani sicurezza e ai palestinesi un futuro di libertà e dignità, nella prospettiva di due Stati che vivano l'uno accanto all'altro all'interno di confini riconosciuti". Un impegno sottoscritto dal ministro degli Esteri e vicepremier, Antonio Tajani: "Continueremo a lavorare per la pace e la stabilita' in Medio Oriente, nella prospettiva di una soluzione politica dei due Stati che garantisca sicurezza di Israele e diritti, dignita' e futuro al popolo palestinese". Di diverso tenore il messaggio, affidato ai social, del vicepremier e leader della Lega, Matteo Salvini: "Nessuna giustificazione, nessuna comprensione per i criminali islamici e il loro odio: vanno combattuti sempre, ovunque, con ogni mezzo necessario". Il leader di Noi Moderati si serve delle parole di patriarca di Gerusalemme dei Latini, Pierbattista Pizzaballa: "Il dolore dei palestinesi non giustifica, non puo' giustificare una cosa del genere. Solo parole ferme e inequivocabili come queste rendono poi credibile il parlare di dialogo, di convivenza di due popoli e due stati, permettono di criticare politiche e azioni anch'esse ingiustificate come quelle dei coloni violenti in Cisgiordania". Orrore per la strage di Hamas e condanna ferma alle violenze contro il popolo palestinese arriva dalla segretaria del Partito Democratico. "Abbiamo sempre detto che quell'orrore non ne giustifica altro. E dobbiamo tenere alta l'attenzione sul fatto che a Gaza i palestinesi continuano a morire sotto le armi dell'esercito israeliano e per mancanza di aiuti umanitari. In Cisgiordania il diritto internazionale viene calpestato quotidianamente dalle violenze dei coloni e dall'allargamento degli insediamenti illegali", sottolinea ancora le leader dem. La risposta al 7 ottobre "non puo' essere un genocidio con oltre 70 mila palestinesi uccisi, oltre 20mila bambini", dice Giuseppe Conte ribadendo l'impegno del suo partito nel "combattere il terrorismo".

A questo, il Presidente Mattarella aggiunge la condanna alle violenze dei coloni Israeliani in Cisgiordania: un "inaccettabile processo di erosione di territori attribuiti all'Autorità Nazionale Palestinese". Da qui il monito affinché sia spezzata questa "spirale di inaudita violenza" e ricreati "i presupposti, oggi profondamente compromessi, della convivenza tra israeliani e palestinesi nella prospettiva 'Due Popoli, Due Stati', per poter vivere pacificamente, fianco a fianco".

E l'impegno: "L'Italia continuerà a sostenere ogni sforzo volto a questo obiettivo". Meloni: "Impegno contro l’antisemitismo" Di "spirale di violenza da interrompere" parla anche la presidente del Consiglio, Giorgia Meloni per la quale la data del 7 ottobre deve rappresentare una pietra d'inciampo contro l'antisemitismo: "Il tempo trascorso", prosegue la premier, "non attenua la gravita' di quei crimini.

Nessuna causa può giustificare il massacro deliberato di innocenti. Ricordarlo significa anche rinnovare l'impegno contro ogni forma di antisemitismo". "Non siamo indifferenti alle sofferenze del popolo di Gaza" Anche la premier, come già il Capo dello Stato, si sofferma sulle "drammatiche e inaccettabili sofferenze degli abitanti di Gaza" e alla "violenza crescente di cui sono vittime i civili palestinesi in Cisgiordania".

Violenze e sofferenze davanti alle quali "non possiamo restare indifferenti". L'orizzonte, ribadisce Meloni, "una pace che garantisca agli israeliani sicurezza e ai palestinesi un futuro di libertà e dignità, nella prospettiva di due Stati che vivano l'uno accanto all'altro all'interno di confini riconosciuti". Un impegno sottoscritto dal ministro degli Esteri e vicepremier, Antonio Tajani: "Continueremo a lavorare per la pace e la stabilita' in Medio Oriente, nella prospettiva di una soluzione politica dei due Stati che garantisca sicurezza di Israele e diritti, dignita' e futuro al popolo palestinese".

Di diverso tenore il messaggio, affidato ai social, del vicepremier e leader della Lega, Matteo Salvini: "Nessuna giustificazione, nessuna comprensione per i criminali islamici e il loro odio: vanno combattuti sempre, ovunque, con ogni mezzo necessario". Il leader di Noi Moderati si serve delle parole di patriarca di Gerusalemme dei Latini, Pierbattista Pizzaballa: "Il dolore dei palestinesi non giustifica, non puo' giustificare una cosa del genere.

Solo parole ferme e inequivocabili come queste rendono poi credibile il parlare di dialogo, di convivenza di due popoli e due stati, permettono di criticare politiche e azioni anch'esse ingiustificate come quelle dei coloni violenti in Cisgiordania". Orrore per la strage di Hamas e condanna ferma alle violenze contro il popolo palestinese arriva dalla segretaria del Partito Democratico. "Abbiamo sempre detto che quell'orrore non ne giustifica altro.

E dobbiamo tenere alta l'attenzione sul fatto che a Gaza i palestinesi continuano a morire sotto le armi dell'esercito israeliano e per mancanza di aiuti umanitari. In Cisgiordania il diritto internazionale viene calpestato quotidianamente dalle violenze dei coloni e dall'allargamento degli insediamenti illegali", sottolinea ancora le leader dem. La risposta al 7 ottobre "non puo' essere un genocidio con oltre 70 mila palestinesi uccisi, oltre 20mila bambini", dice Giuseppe Conte ribadendo l'impegno del suo partito nel "combattere il terrorismo".

articles.title: Tre anni dopo l’attacco di Hamas a Israele
articles.summary: Gli eventi seguiti agli attentati del 7 ottobre 2023 hanno precipitato il Medio Oriente in conflitti, fratture e tragedie dalla Striscia di Gaza allo Yemen
articles.preview: Come le scosse di assestamento di un terremoto, che possono arrivare anche molto tempo dopo il sisma iniziale, il 7 ottobre 2023 continua a scuotere il Medio Oriente. A tre anni di distanza da quel giorno fatidico, il paesaggio regionale è segnato dalle guerre, dalle fratture e dai conflitti senza soluzione: da Rafah, nella Striscia di Gaza, a Hormuz, nel golfo Persico; da Naqura, nel sud del Libano, a Moka, in Yemen. Tutto questo, evidentemente, non è cominciato il 7 ottobre.
articles.body:
Come le scosse di assestamento di un terremoto, che possono arrivare anche molto tempo dopo il sisma iniziale, il 7 ottobre 2023 continua a scuotere il Medio Oriente. A tre anni di distanza da quel giorno fatidico, il paesaggio regionale è segnato dalle guerre, dalle fratture e dai conflitti senza soluzione: da Rafah, nella Striscia di Gaza, a Hormuz, nel golfo Persico; da Naqura, nel sud del Libano, a Moka, in Yemen.

Tutto questo, evidentemente, non è cominciato il 7 ottobre. La dinamica si era già messa in moto da tempo e ognuno dei conflitti citati ha vissuto numerosi episodi molto prima del 2023. Tuttavia, l’attacco di Hamas contro le comunità del sud di Israele – con il suo carattere inedito, la sua portata, il gran numero di vittime civili, la cattura di numerosi ostaggi e le falle nella sicurezza dello stato ebraico – è stato un punto di rottura in questa regione martoriata.

Fin dai primi giorni è apparso chiaro che Israele avrebbe risposto subito al più grave attacco terroristico dalla sua nascita. Sapevamo che questa risposta sarebbe stata sproporzionata, perché questa è la dottrina dell’esercito israeliano. Presto abbiamo scoperto anche che sarebbe stata impietosa, sull’onda della sete di vendetta e dell’idea che a Gaza non ci fossero “innocenti”.

Ma a pagarne il prezzo non sono stati solo gli abitanti della Striscia. Anche il Libano è stato trascinato nella guerra quando Hezbollah, movimento armato sciita e filoiraniano, ha voluto manifestare la propria solidarietà ad Hamas. Nel 2024, e poi di nuovo quest’anno, il Libano si è ritrovato sotto le bombe israeliane, mentre gli abitanti del nord di Israele hanno dovuto affrontare i razzi di Hezbollah. Oggi il Libano è in un’impasse, incapace di disarmare Hezbollah e alle prese con un’occupazione prolungata del sud del paese da parte delle forze israeliane. Una tragedia, per uno stato ormai esangue.

La vera svolta, però, è arrivata con la guerra scatenata da Israele e dagli Stati Uniti contro l’Iran, con una violenza mai vista in passato. Prima c’è stata la cosiddetta guerra dei dodici giorni, nel 2025. Poi, con bombardamenti ancora più massicci, è arrivata l’offensiva dello scorso febbraio, che ha decapitato il regime iraniano, uccidendo la guida suprema Ali Khamenei.

Da allora Donald Trump, con la sua incompetenza, si è impantanato sempre di più in una guerra da cui non riesce a uscire e che ha intaccato la credibilità della potenza statunitense nella regione.

Una soluzione a breve termine per questi conflitti non esiste. Al contrario, la guerra si sta allargando allo Yemen, con il coinvolgimento dell’Arabia Saudita che difende le sue esportazioni petrolifere. Nel frattempo la violenza dei coloni in Cisgiordania continua a crescere, il calvario di Gaza prosegue e un’intera regione vive il terzo anno di tempesta.

L’unico elemento che potrebbe fermare questa spirale infernale è l’esito delle elezioni israeliane, previste fra tre settimane. Ma davvero gli elettori dello stato ebraico decideranno di punire il primo ministro Benjamin Netanyahu per la sua responsabilità in queste tragedie? O si affideranno ancora una volta a lui (ciecamente, verrebbe da dire)?

Gli oppositori di Netanyahu non sono certo moderati sulla questione palestinese, ma resta il fatto che una sua eventuale uscita di scena, insieme alla sua coalizione di estrema destra, cambierebbe le carte in tavola, permettendo, forse, di voltare finalmente la pagina tragica aperta il 7 ottobre 2023.

(Traduzione di Andrea Sparacino)

articles.body:
Mecka AI, a startup that collects and analyzes human motion data to train humanoid robots and other kinds of robots, announced it has raised a $60 million Series B round led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Microsoft’s venture fund M12, and others. TechCrunch had previously reported that the startup was nearing a new funding round at a $500 million valuation.

Founded in 2024, the startup intends to do for robotics what Scale AI, Mercor, Surge, and other data-labeling companies have done for LLMs. Those companies supply the human-generated data these systems learn from. Mecka pays people to record themselves doing everyday tasks, like making coffee or fixing cars, while wearing body sensors and using smartphones.

Other startups that collect real-world data for robot training include XDOF, which was in talks to raise a Series B round at a $1.2 billion valuation according to TechCrunch’s previous reporting. Human-data platforms that began with LLMs are also expanding into robotics, such as Scale AI and Micro1.

articles.body:
Nous Research, the startup developing the open source Hermes Agent, has raised a $90 million Series B at a $1.5 billion valuation, confirming TechCrunch’s earlier reporting.

The round was led by Robot Ventures, with participation from other backers including Nvidia, Union Square Ventures, Menlo Ventures, Samsung, and 1789 Capital, where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. The new financing brings the three-year-old startup’s total funding to $158 million.

Popular among developers and individuals, the open source Hermes Agent has been cloned more than 24 million times, driving roughly 2.5% of global AI token usage, according to the startup’s estimates.

The capital will fund Nous Research’s push into the enterprise sector with “Hermes for Businesses,” allowing companies to deploy customized AI agents that can handle multi-step workflows while keeping their data private and secure.

Nous was at roughly $36 million in annualized revenue by mid-September 2026 and expects to pass $100 million before the end of 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported.

articles.body:
Back in June, Nvidia announced that it had secured agreements with Microsoft and a host of other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready PCs for Windows based on its RTX Spark chip, but details on the machines were scant at the time.

On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city’s Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra. The PC comes in two base models, one that starts at $2,600 and one with a more powerful chip that starts at $3,700. Prices rise from there with options for more memory and storage, up to $5,900. (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.)

Microsoft also revealed its new workstation powered by the RTX Spark chip: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, which starts priced at $6,000 and comes equipped with Microsoft dev tools like VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7.

The pitch for both this PC and workstation is that they are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free) with the CPU, GPU, unified memory, and other hardware modifications, like superior cooling, necessary to handle them.

Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called “Execution Containers.” This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event.

Nadella explained: “One of the things we realized in the last 3-4 years is that just having a model doesn’t do much for anything. You really do need to orchestrate, and you need to have memory outside of the model. You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space.”

He added that Microsoft is enabling that “not just for our apps but apps for anyone’s agent. That’s what the Windows platform is all about going forward.”

The devices are clearly aimed at developers, so much so that Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro, as Macs have become a popular choice for developers and AI agent enthusiasts, particularly in Silicon Valley.

Still, these Surface PCs, with such powerful graphics processing, are also capable of content creation, video processing, and gaming, the company promises.

Microsoft wasn’t the only PC company to announce the specs for its new Nvidia-RTX Spark AI Windows PCs on Wednesday. Dell also announced the details of its previously announced Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition PC. It’s available for preorder now for a later October delivery at Best Buy, priced at $3,800.

articles.body:
OpenAI is launching a new Intelligent UI feature in ChatGPT that allows the chatbot to answer your questions with interactive visuals. The update, which is rolling out to all users alongside GPT-6, gives ChatGPT the ability to combine a text response with diagrams, charts, forms, tappable buttons, and more.

With GPT-6, the chatbot’s responses can include interactive responses directly inside your conversation.

In a blog post explaining the change, OpenAI says it trained GPT-6 when to generate interactive visuals over text, as well as how to format them in its response. An example shared by OpenAI shows how ChatGPT might show a diagram of a seven-speed bicycle if you ask about its design, complete with interactive buttons that highlight different parts.

Another shows how ChatGPT can teach you to play Mahjong by generating visuals of each tile and placing them into categories that you can scroll through. You can also ask ChatGPT to generate tools for different tasks, such as a retirement savings calculator, retro game, or bill splitter. It will then generate the tool in-line with its response.

OpenAI announced its first GPT-6 models last month, but now it’s bringing the Sol and Luna versions to ChatGPT. In addition to enabling Intelligent UI, OpenAI says its GPT-6 allows ChatGPT to perform better web searches and provide quicker, partial answers to users while it gathers information. The company notes that GPT-6 “showed stronger resistance to attempts to bypass its safety training” as well.

GPT-6 with Intelligent UI is rolling out globally to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users starting today, but will expand to Go and free tiers on Thursday. While higher-tier subscribers will gain access to the mid-range GPT-6 Sol model, Go and free users will get to use the more efficient GPT-6 Luna.

articles.body:
The first array of laptops powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip are designed to compete with high-end MacBook Pros — and they’ve got some high-end prices to match.

Prices start much lower, but 128GB of unified memory is going to really cost you.

The flagship Surface Laptop Ultra and RTX Spark laptops from Dell, Lenovo, MSI, HP, and Asus start as low as $2,599 for configurations with an 18-core CPU, 24GB of unified memory, and 512GB of storage. That’s close in price to a similarly specced 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro chip, though Apple includes 1TB of storage. But the prices for both RTX Spark and Apple laptops of course go much, much higher.

Of the pricing we’ve seen so far, a kitted-out Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark laptop with a 20-core chip, 128GB of unified memory, and 2TB of storage costs up to $6,999.99. We don’t yet know the full breadth of configuration options for Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra, as the preorder page only has an email sign-up box to get updates, but a 48GB model on Best Buy costs $3,999.99.

Wildly expensive laptops aren’t really anything new: you can configure a 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Max chip to nearly $10,000 if you max out all options. But the first volley of RTX Spark options are obviously aimed at the high-end side of creators and local AI users. And RAMageddon certainly isn’t helping make this any easier on peoples’ wallets.

Will they be worth it? We’ll find out soon. The Surface Laptop Ultra and other RTX Spark laptops are launching this month — as early as October 16th.
